question: Milling removes metal using a…
explanation: Milling uses a rotating multi-point cutting tool called a milling cutter.

question: In milling, which element rotates and which is fed?
options: The work rotates; the cutter is fed along it
The cutter rotates; the work is fed against it
Both the cutter and the work reciprocate
Neither rotates; the table only vibrates
explanation: The milling cutter rotates at a fixed position while the work (table) is fed into it.

question: In milling, the movement of the work (table) towards the cutter is called…
explanation: The notes define the movement of the metal (work) as feeding.

question: How does a milling cutter remove metal?
options: The metal is melted by friction at the teeth
Abrasive grains on its face rub the metal away
One continuous chip is removed in each pass
Each tooth removes a small chip in every revolution
explanation: Each tooth of the multi-point cutter takes a small chip during every rotation.

question: Why is the milling machine called one of the most versatile machine tools?
options: It can produce flat surfaces, slots, gears and complex shapes
It can produce only cylindrical parts quickly
It needs no cutting tool for most operations
It removes metal only by abrasive grinding
explanation: With different cutters and attachments (like the dividing head), a milling machine makes flat surfaces, slots, keyways, gears and contours.

question: Milling cutters are generally made of…
explanation: The lecture states milling cutters are generally made of HSS.

question: Machining (including milling) is best described as a…
options: Additive process that builds up layers of material
Subtractive process that removes excess material
Forming process that shapes metal without chips
Joining process that fuses two parts together
explanation: Machining is subtractive: excess material is removed to get the required geometry and finish.

question: Up milling is also known as…
explanation: Up milling = conventional milling; down milling = climb milling.

question: Down milling is also known as…
explanation: Down milling = climb milling: the cutter rotation is in the same direction as the feed.

question: In up milling, the direction of cutter rotation at the cut is…
options: The same as the direction of feed
Opposite to the direction of feed
explanation: In up (conventional) milling the cutter rotates against the feed.

question: In which milling method is the chip thickness zero at the start of the cut and maximum at the end?
explanation: Up milling: chip thickness minimum at the start, maximum at the end. Down milling: the reverse.

question: In down milling, the chip thickness is…
options: Maximum at the start of the cut and minimum at the end
Zero at the start of the cut and maximum at the end
Constant from the start to the end of the cut
Zero throughout, since the teeth only rub
explanation: In down (climb) milling the tooth enters at maximum chip thickness and leaves at minimum.

question: Which is an ADVANTAGE of up milling?
options: It needs the least clamping force on the work
Scale on the work surface does not affect tool life much
The cutter never chatters, even with light clamping
It gives the best surface finish of all methods
explanation: In up milling the tooth starts under the scale, so surface scale does not damage the cutter much.

question: Which is a DISADVANTAGE of up milling?
options: It puts maximum radial load on the arbor at entry
It cannot be used on scaled work
The cutter tends to lift the work, so firm clamping is needed
explanation: In up milling the upward cutting force tends to pull the work up off the table, and the tool tends to chatter.

question: Which milling method gives a better surface finish and less radial pressure on the arbor?
explanation: Down milling gives a better finish, puts less radial pressure on the arbor and needs less power.

question: Why is down milling NOT suitable for workpieces with surface scale?
options: The tooth hits the hard scale first, reducing tool life
The work is lifted off the table by the cutter
The chip thickness becomes zero at the scale
It needs a dividing head to be fitted to the table
explanation: In down milling each tooth enters at maximum chip thickness through the hard scale, which wears the cutter.

question: Compared with down milling, up milling…
options: Gives a rougher surface and needs more power
Has chip thickness maximum at the start
Gives a smoother surface and needs less power
explanation: Up milling rubs at entry, so the finish is rougher and the power is higher; down milling is the reverse.
ref: Milling TA slides s.8; Milling lecture slide 7

question: Up milling is preferred when the machine has significant backlash in the table feed screw. Why?
options: The cutter pulls the table forward into the cut
The cutting force pushes against the feed, taking up backlash
The chip thickness is maximum at entry, which helps
It removes the need to clamp the work at all
explanation: In up milling the cutter opposes the feed, so the table is kept pressed against the screw. In climb milling the cutter can pull the table into the backlash.
ref: Milling lecture slide 5; Milling TA slides s.8

question: Plain (slab) milling produces…
options: A slot, using the end teeth of the cutter
Gear teeth, using a form cutter on the arbor
A V-groove, using a double-angle cutter
A flat surface, with teeth on the periphery of the cutter
explanation: Plain milling (slab milling) produces a flat surface with the peripheral teeth; the cutter axis is parallel to the surface.

question: In plain (slab) milling, the cutter axis is…
explanation: In slab milling the axis of the cutter is parallel to the surface being milled.

question: Which cutter is used for slab milling (as given in the ME-106 notes)?
explanation: The notes call the helical plain milling cutter a "nick cutter", used for slab cutting.

question: In face milling, the cutter axis is…
explanation: Face milling uses a cutter whose axis is perpendicular to the surface being produced.

question: In end milling, when the cutter diameter is less than the work width, the result is a…
options: Flat face across the whole part
explanation: An end mill smaller than the work width cuts a slot.

question: Machining two parallel vertical faces at once, using two side cutters on one arbor, is called…
explanation: Straddle milling uses two side (side-and-face) cutters separated by spacing collars.

question: In straddle milling, the distance between the two cutters is set by…
explanation: Spacing collars (spacers) between the cutters on the arbor fix the distance.

question: Straddle milling is commonly used to produce…
options: Spur gear teeth on a blank
explanation: Two parallel faces at a time make square or hexagonal shapes, e.g. bolt heads.

question: Using several cutters (same or different) on one arbor to machine several surfaces at once is called…
explanation: Gang milling mounts a gang of cutters together on the arbor to machine several surfaces simultaneously.

question: Gang milling is widely used because it…
options: Saves machining time in repetitive work
explanation: Machining several surfaces in one pass saves time, which suits repetitive (production) work.

question: In gang milling, the cutting speed is calculated from…
options: The cutter with the smallest diameter
The cutter with the largest diameter
The average of all cutter diameters
explanation: All cutters turn at the same rpm, so the largest cutter has the highest surface speed. The speed is chosen for that cutter.

question: Form milling is mainly used for…
options: Cutting gear teeth and other profiles
explanation: Form milling uses cutters whose teeth match the required profile, e.g. gear-tooth spaces.

question: Compared with plain milling, the cutting rate in form milling is…
explanation: The lecture states the cutting rate in form milling is 20–30% less than in plain milling.

question: Producing a V-block (surfaces at an angle to the spindle axis) is an example of…
explanation: Angular milling produces surfaces at an angle other than 90° to the spindle axis, e.g. V-blocks.

question: Which cutters can be used to cut slots or keyways?
options: End mill, slot drill or side-and-face cutter
explanation: Slots and keyways are cut with end mills, slot drills, side-and-face cutters or slitting saws.

question: Which of these is NOT one of the milling operations listed in the ME-106 lecture?
explanation: The lecture lists plain, face, end, straddle, form, gang and angular milling. Knurling is a lathe operation.

question: A milling cutter with cutting edges on both sides as well as on its periphery is a…
explanation: The wall chart describes the side-and-face cutter as cutting on its face and both sides.

question: Which of these cutters is NOT shown on the "Milling cutters" wall chart in the ME-106 milling lab?
explanation: The chart shows plain, helical plain, side-and-face, interlocking side, half-side and staggered-tooth side cutters.

question: Which cutter is used to cut T-slots like those in machine tables?
explanation: A T-slot cutter makes the wide bottom of a T-slot after a narrow slot has been cut.

question: A thin milling cutter used for narrow slots or for cutting off is a…
explanation: Slitting saws are thin discs with fine teeth for narrow slots and cutting off.

question: A large cylindrical cutter with teeth only on its outside, used for wide flat surfaces, is the…
explanation: The slab (plain) cutter cuts large flat surfaces with its peripheral teeth.

question: Which cutter is pipe-shaped with teeth on the inside and is used to cut rods to size?
explanation: A hollow milling cutter has internal teeth and machines round rods to size.

question: Which cutter has a rounded tip and is used for 3-D contouring of curved surfaces?
explanation: A ball-nose end mill has a hemispherical tip for 3-D contours; a plain end mill cuts on its tip and sides.

question: A large cutter, often with inserts, that cuts with its bottom face to give flat smooth surfaces is a…
explanation: A face-mill cutter cuts with its face (bottom) and gives flat, smooth surfaces.

question: Which cutter is used to machine dovetail grooves?
explanation: A dovetail cutter has angled sides that produce the dovetail shape.

question: A simple bar holding a single cutting tip, used for large smooth flat areas, is a…
explanation: A fly cutter is a single-point milling tool for light finishing of large flat areas.

question: A roughing end mill has wavy (serrated) cutting edges. It is used for…
options: Removing a lot of material quickly with a rough finish
Final finishing of involute gear teeth
Cutting very thin slots and parting off
Polishing surfaces to a mirror finish
explanation: Serrated edges break the chips up, allowing heavy stock removal; the finish is rough.

question: Cutters shaped to a specific profile, used to make gears or threads, are called…
explanation: Formed cutters have teeth shaped to the profile they produce.

question: Which cutter is used in the ME-106 lab to cut the spur gear teeth?
explanation: The milling TA slides and the lab tool photo show an involute gear (form) cutter for cutting spur gear teeth.

question: Why does a set of involute gear cutters contain several cutters for one diametral pitch?
options: Each cutter is for a different speed
Each cutter is for a different depth
Each cutter covers a range of tooth numbers
Each cutter is for a different material
explanation: The tooth-space shape changes with the number of teeth, so each cutter in a set covers a range of tooth numbers.

question: Which of these is a term from milling-cutter nomenclature?
explanation: Cutter nomenclature includes outside diameter, hole, keyway, face of tooth, land, rake and clearance angles, depth of tooth, pitch and helix angle. Tang (file), clapper (shaper) and quill (lathe) are other tools.

question: On a milling cutter, the keyway in the bore is used to…
options: Drive the cutter from the arbor through a key
Hold the coolant near the teeth
Set the helix angle of the teeth
explanation: The key in the cutter keyway and arbor keyway transmits the drive.
ref: Milling lecture slide 16; Milling wall chart

question: Which of these is NOT a type of milling machine?
explanation: Milling machines are column-and-knee (hand, horizontal, vertical, universal), fixed-bed/planer type and CNC. Capstan is a type of lathe.

question: Column-and-knee milling machines are classed as horizontal or vertical according to the…
options: Type of coolant used on the work
Direction in which the knee moves
explanation: Horizontal and vertical refer to the axis of the spindle/cutter.

question: In a horizontal milling machine, the spindle axis is…
explanation: A horizontal mill has its spindle (and arbor) parallel to the table.

question: Cutters on a horizontal milling machine are mounted on the…
explanation: Horizontal machines use arbor-mounted cutters; vertical machines use end mills and face mills in the spindle.
ref: Milling lecture slide 18; Milling wall chart

question: Which cutters are normally used on a vertical milling machine?
explanation: A vertical mill holds end mills and face mills directly in the vertical spindle.

question: Which statement correctly compares horizontal and vertical milling machines?
options: Horizontal: higher metal removal; vertical: more versatile for slots and profiles
Horizontal: more versatile for profiles; vertical: heavier metal removal
Both machines have identical uses and use the same cutters
Vertical machines cannot cut slots; horizontal machines cannot face
explanation: Horizontal mills take heavy cuts on large flat surfaces; vertical mills are more versatile for slots, holes and complex profiles.

question: Which part of a column-and-knee milling machine moves up and down on the column?
explanation: The knee slides vertically on the column (vertical feed) and carries the saddle and table.

question: The knee of a milling machine is raised and lowered by the…
explanation: The elevating screw (worked by the knee elevating handle) raises and lowers the knee.

question: On a column-and-knee mill, cross movement (towards or away from the column) is given by the…
explanation: The saddle moves on the knee for cross feed; the table moves on the saddle longitudinally.

question: The outer end of the arbor on a horizontal milling machine is supported by the…
options: Arbor support hanging from the overarm
explanation: The arbor support, carried on the overarm, steadies the outer end of the arbor.

question: Which part houses the spindle drive and carries the overarm?
explanation: The column is the main vertical casting on the base; it houses the spindle drive and carries the overarm.

question: Which of these parts is shown on the column-and-knee milling machine wall chart in the ME-106 lab?
explanation: The chart lists base, elevating screw, knee, knee elevating handle, cross-feed handle, saddle, table, front brace, arbor support, arbor, overhanging arm, cutter, column, cone pulley and telescopic feed shaft.

question: Which parts are typical of a vertical milling machine?
options: Headstock and tailstock with live centre
explanation: A vertical mill has a milling head on a ram (overarm), with the spindle in a quill.

question: In a bed-type milling machine, the table is…
options: Mounted on a fixed bed and moves only horizontally
Carried on a knee that moves up and down
explanation: The bed-type machine replaces the knee with a large bed; the table moves only horizontally.

question: What type of milling machine is used for the gear job in the ME-106 lab?
options: Hand milling machine without power feed
CNC vertical machining centre with ATC
explanation: The log sheets list a universal horizontal milling machine (column-and-knee type).

question: Which of these is NOT a main component of a horizontal milling machine?
explanation: Horizontal mill parts: base, column, knee, saddle, table, spindle, arbor, overarm, arbor support. The clapper box belongs to a shaper.

question: In milling, indexing means…
options: Measuring the diameter of the cutter
Setting the cutting speed of the spindle
Dividing the work periphery into equal divisions
Clamping the work firmly in the vice
explanation: Indexing divides the periphery into equal (or unequal) parts by rotating the work by a precise angle between cuts.

question: An index plate is…
options: A plate with circles of equally spaced holes
A table having T-slots for clamping
A gear wheel having exactly 40 teeth
A graduated dial fitted on the knee
explanation: The index plate has several hole circles; the index pin engages these holes.

question: The worm and worm wheel of a standard dividing head give a ratio of…
explanation: The worm wheel has 40 teeth and the worm is single-start, so the ratio is 40 : 1.

question: How many turns of the index crank rotate the work once on a standard dividing head?
explanation: 40 turns of the crank make one turn of the work spindle (40 : 1).

question: Which of these is NOT an indexing method?
explanation: The methods are direct, simple, compound and differential indexing. Straddle is a milling set-up.

question: Direct indexing is also called…
explanation: Direct indexing is the simplest method, also called rapid indexing.

question: In direct indexing…
options: Change gears drive the plate from the spindle
The worm is disengaged and the plate is turned by hand
The worm drives the spindle through 40 : 1
Two hole circles are used one after the other
explanation: In direct (rapid) indexing the worm is disengaged; the direct plate (24, 30 or 36 holes) is turned by hand.

question: Which hole circles are used on a direct indexing plate?
explanation: The lecture states direct indexing uses a plate with 24, 30 or 36 holes.

question: Using direct indexing on a 24-hole plate, how many holes are moved for each side of a square?
explanation: 24 holes / 4 divisions = 6 holes each time (lecture example).

question: Using direct indexing on a 24-hole plate, how many holes are moved for each face of a hexagon?
explanation: 24 / 6 = 4 holes per division.
ref: Milling lecture slide 24; Milling lecture slide 23

question: In simple (plain) indexing, the crank movement per division is…
explanation: With a 40 : 1 dividing head, crank turns = 40/N. A common mistake is to use 40 × N or N/40.

question: Simple indexing for N = 7 divisions needs…
options: 5 full turns + 35 holes on the 49-hole circle
7 full turns + 5 holes on the 49-hole circle
5 full turns + 5 holes on the 7-hole circle
explanation: 40/7 = 5 5/7. There is no 7-hole circle, so 5/7 = 35/49: 5 turns + 35 holes on the 49-hole circle (lecture example).

question: Compound indexing involves…
options: Disengaging the worm and turning the plate directly by hand
Moving the crank on one circle and then the plate itself on another circle
Using change gears between the spindle and the index plate
Moving only the sector arms while the crank stays fixed
explanation: Compound indexing combines crank movement on one hole circle with movement of the plate (rear lock pin released) on another.

question: Differential indexing is used when…
options: Simple indexing cannot give the required division
explanation: Differential indexing gears the spindle to the plate to obtain divisions not possible with simple indexing (e.g. some primes).

question: Which hole circles are on index plate 2 (Brown & Sharpe) used in the ME-106 lab?
Which of these is a hole circle on index plate 3 (Brown & Sharpe)?
explanation: Plate 3 has 37, 39, 41, 43, 47 and 49 holes.

question: What is the purpose of the sector arms on a dividing head?
options: To change the 40 : 1 ratio of the dividing head
To span the required number of holes so they need not be counted each time
To lock the work spindle firmly while cutting
To engage the worm with the worm wheel when indexing
explanation: The sector arms are set to the needed number of hole spaces, which speeds up indexing and avoids counting errors.

question: While indexing a gear, the index crank should never be turned backwards because…
options: Backlash in the worm drive will spoil the division
The index plate will fall off its shaft
The cutter rotation will be reversed
The coolant supply will stop automatically
explanation: The 2025 log sheet says not to rotate the index-plate handle in the opposite direction; reversing introduces backlash errors.

question: Diametral pitch (DP) is defined as…
options: Number of teeth per inch of pitch-circle diameter
Number of teeth per inch of circumference
Pitch-circle diameter per tooth in mm
explanation: DP = N / D_pitch (inches). (The notebook's "teeth / circumference" is wrong. See corrections.md.)

question: The formula for the outside (blank) diameter of a spur gear in the DP system is…
explanation: OD = (N + 2)/DP: the pitch diameter N/DP plus two addenda of 1/DP each.

question: Pitch-circle diameter in the DP system is…
explanation: D_pitch = N/DP. Adding two addenda (2/DP) gives the outside diameter.

question: In the DP system, the addendum equals…
explanation: Addendum = 1/DP, dedendum = 1.157/DP, clearance = 0.157/DP.

question: In the DP system, the dedendum equals…
explanation: Dedendum = addendum + clearance = 1/DP + 0.157/DP = 1.157/DP.

question: In standard gear terminology, 2.157/DP is the…
explanation: Whole depth = 1/DP + 1.157/DP = 2.157/DP. Standard working depth (two addenda) = 2/DP. Our lab calls 2.157/DP the "working depth".

question: In standard (textbook) terminology, the working depth of a gear tooth equals…
explanation: Working depth = sum of the addenda of two mating gears = 2/DP. Whole depth = 2.157/DP (called "working depth" in our lab).

question: In the ME-106 milling lab, the depth to which the gear teeth are cut ("working depth") is calculated as…
explanation: The lab board and log sheet use W.D. = 2.157/DP. (The lab calls 2.157/DP the "working depth"; textbooks call it the whole depth.)

question: Circular pitch in the DP system is…
explanation: Circular pitch = π × D_pitch / N = π/DP.

question: The relation between module m (mm) and diametral pitch DP (per inch) is…
explanation: Module = pitch diameter (mm) / N, and 1 inch = 25.4 mm, so m = 25.4/DP.

question: A spur gear has teeth that are…
options: Cut on the surface of a cone
Straight and parallel to the axis of rotation
Cut on the inside of a ring
Inclined at an angle to the axis
explanation: A spur gear is the simplest and most common gear, with straight teeth parallel to the axis.

question: Which of these is NOT a spur gear nomenclature term?
explanation: Spur gears have straight teeth, so they have no helix angle. Addendum, dedendum, pitch circle, circular pitch and tooth thickness are spur-gear terms.

question: Spur and helical gears connect shafts that are…
explanation: Spur, helical and herringbone gears all connect parallel shafts.

question: Compared with spur gears, helical gears…
options: Are noisier and produce no axial thrust
Convert rotary motion into linear motion
Run more smoothly and quietly but produce axial thrust
explanation: Inclined teeth engage gradually: smoother and quieter, but with an axial thrust component.

question: Why are double-helical (herringbone) gears used?
options: The opposite helices cancel the axial thrust
They convert rotation into straight-line motion
explanation: Two opposite-hand helices produce equal and opposite axial thrusts that cancel.

question: Bevel gears are used to connect shafts that are…
explanation: Bevel gears are conical and connect intersecting shafts.

question: A worm and worm wheel connect shafts that are…
explanation: The worm and worm wheel connect perpendicular, non-intersecting shafts and give a large reduction (40 : 1 in the dividing head).

question: Which gear arrangement converts rotary motion into straight-line motion?
explanation: A pinion rolling on a straight rack turns rotation into linear motion. The rack is a gear of infinite radius.

question: In an internal gear…
options: Teeth are cut on the surface of a cone
Teeth are cut on the inside of a ring
Teeth form a continuous screw thread
Teeth are cut along a straight bar
explanation: An internal gear has inward-facing teeth and meshes with an external pinion on a parallel shaft.

question: Crossed helical (spiral) gears are used for shafts that are…
explanation: Crossed helical gears connect skew (non-parallel, non-intersecting) shafts.

question: Which gear pair gives the largest speed reduction in a single stage?
explanation: A single-start worm advances the wheel only one tooth per revolution, so ratios like 40 : 1 are easy.
ref: Milling lecture slide 22; Milling lecture slide 22, s.25

question: What is the objective of the ME-106 milling job?
options: To cut a keyway along a shaft with an end mill
To face-mill a rectangular block to 73 mm
To cut a helical gear from a round steel bar
To make a spur gear from a circular workpiece by milling
explanation: The milling log sheet objective: to make a spur gear using milling operations from a circular workpiece.

question: What is the workpiece material for the ME-106 spur gear?
explanation: The gear blank is an aluminium circular disc with a centre hole.

question: What diametral pitch is used for the ME-106 gear?
explanation: The lab board and log sheet give DP = 16 (teeth per inch).

question: What is the outside (blank) diameter of the ME-106 gear?
explanation: The 2025 board and log sheet give OD = 1½ in with DP 16.

question: For the ME-106 gear, OD = 1½ in and DP = 16. How many teeth does the gear have?
explanation: OD = (N + 2)/DP → N = OD × DP − 2 = 1.5 × 16 − 2 = 22. Forgetting the −2 gives 24.

question: For the 22-tooth ME-106 gear, how is the index crank moved for each tooth?
options: 2 full turns + 18 holes on the 21-hole circle
1 full turn + 27 holes on the 33-hole circle
1 full turn + 9 holes on the 33-hole circle
explanation: 40/22 = 1 18/22 = 1 9/11. Multiply 9/11 by 3/3 = 27/33, so 1 turn + 27 holes on the 33-hole circle (plate 2). 40 × 22 = 880 is the classic mistake.

question: Which index plate is used for the ME-106 22-tooth gear?
explanation: 9/11 = 27/33, and the 33-hole circle is on plate 2.

question: For the ME-106 gear (DP 16), what depth is set for cutting the teeth, using the lab formula?
explanation: 2.157/16 = 0.1348 in = 3.42 mm. 0.125 in is 2/DP (textbook working depth); 0.0625 is the addendum; 0.1963 is the circular pitch. (The lab calls 2.157/DP the "working depth"; textbooks call it the whole depth.)

question: For the ME-106 gear (22 teeth, DP 16), what is the pitch-circle diameter?
explanation: D_pitch = N/DP = 22/16 = 1.375 in. 1.5 in is the outside diameter.

question: For the ME-106 gear (DP 16), what is the circular pitch?
explanation: Circular pitch = π/DP = 3.1416/16 = 0.196 in.
ref: Theory: Machinery's Handbook; Manufacturing notes p.3

question: For DP 16, what is the addendum?
explanation: Addendum = 1/DP = 1/16 = 0.0625 in. 0.0723 is the dedendum (1.157/16).
ref: Theory: Machinery's Handbook; Manufacturing notes p.3

question: What module (mm) is equivalent to DP 16?
ref: Theory: Machinery's Handbook; Manufacturing notes p.3

question: Practice: a gear blank of OD 1 in is cut with DP 16. How many teeth?
explanation: N = OD × DP − 2 = 16 − 2 = 14 (worked example in the notes).

question: Practice: indexing for a 14-tooth gear on a standard dividing head is…
options: 1 full turn + 27 holes on the 33-hole circle
2 full turns + 6 holes on the 21-hole circle
2 full turns + 18 holes on the 21-hole circle
explanation: 40/14 = 2 6/7 = 2 18/21, so 2 turns + 18 holes on the 21-hole circle.
ref: Manufacturing notes p.3–4; Milling lecture slide 25

question: How many degrees does the work rotate for one full turn of the index crank?
explanation: One turn of the work (360°) takes 40 crank turns, so 360/40 = 9° per crank turn.

question: Simple indexing for 36 divisions can be done as…
options: 1 full turn + 4 holes on the 18-hole circle
1 full turn + 1 hole on the 36-hole circle
1 full turn + 2 holes on the 18-hole circle
explanation: 40/36 = 1 1/9 = 1 2/18. So 1 turn + 2 holes on the 18-hole circle (plate 1). There is no 36-hole circle on the simple-indexing plates.
ref: Milling lecture slide 25; Manufacturing notes p.4

question: For a 40-tooth gear, the index crank movement per tooth is…
explanation: 40/40 = 1 turn per division.

question: A gear blank of 2 in OD is to be cut with DP 12. How many teeth will the gear have?
How is the ME-106 gear blank held during milling?
options: On a mandrel between the dividing head and the tailstock
On the magnetic chuck of the table
In a machine vice clamped to the table
In a 4-jaw chuck on the milling table
explanation: The aluminium blank is mounted on a mandrel (shaft) supported by the dividing head and tailstock.

question: Which item from the ME-106 milling tool list holds the gear blank?
explanation: The blank is mounted on a mandrel. The catch pin locks the index crank, and the file is used for deburring.

question: Which of these is NOT in the ME-106 milling log-sheet tool lists?
explanation: The milling log sheets list the milling machine, index plate, chalk, catch pin, shaft, mandrel, worm wheel, tailstock, rough flat file, bench vice, coolant and calipers.

question: In the ME-106 milling lab, what is the rough flat file used for?
explanation: After cutting, the gear is polished/deburred with a file.
ref: Log Sheets ME-106 p.9; Milling Log Sheet #1

question: Which tool is used to measure the outside diameter of the gear blank?
explanation: The outer diameter of the blank is measured with an outside caliper (with a steel rule).

question: Which tools does the notebook list for the milling job?
options: Emery paper, wire and pumice powder
Outside caliper, mandrel and chuck key
explanation: The notes list outside caliper, mandrel and chuck key for the milling job.

question: Which item was photographed among the ME-106 milling lab tools?
explanation: The milling tools photo shows a flat file, outside caliper, index plate, steel rule, involute gear cutter, double-ended spanner, finished gears and a gear-train model.

question: What is the FIRST step of the ME-106 milling procedure?
options: Calculate the number of teeth from OD and DP
Switch on the machine and the coolant
Polish the finished gear with a file
Cut the first tooth space on the blank
explanation: Step 1: calculate the number of teeth using the outside diameter and diametral pitch.

question: In the ME-106 milling procedure, what is calculated immediately after the number of teeth?
options: The taper angle for the gear blank
The grinding ratio of the cutter wear
The working depth (2.157/DP) and the indexing (40/N)
The cutting speed of the cutter in m/min
explanation: Step 2: calculate the working depth and the index.

question: Which step comes immediately after calculating the depth and indexing?
options: Polish the gear with the rough flat file
Remove the mandrel from the dividing head
Measure the finished gear with a caliper
Fix the appropriate index plate on the dividing head
explanation: Step 3: fix the index plate that has the required hole circle (33 holes for our gear).

question: What is the correct sequence of the ME-106 milling procedure?
options: Clamp blank and start → cut and index repeatedly → calculate N → fix index plate → file the gear → calculate depth & index
Fix index plate → file the gear → calculate N → clamp blank and start → cut and index repeatedly → calculate depth & index
Calculate N → calculate depth & index → fix index plate → clamp blank and start → cut and index repeatedly → file the gear
Calculate depth & index → cut and index repeatedly → clamp blank and start → calculate N → fix index plate → file the gear
explanation: Log sheet: calculate teeth; calculate working depth and index; fix index plate; clamp workpiece and switch on machine and coolant; cut, return and index, repeat; polish with file.
ref: Log Sheets ME-106 p.9; Milling Log Sheet #1

question: After clamping the blank, what is switched on along with the machine?
explanation: Step 4: clamp the workpiece tightly, then switch on the machine and the coolant.

question: How are successive tooth spaces cut on the ME-106 gear?
options: Cut all the spaces at once with a gang of cutters
Cut one space, bring the table back, index the crank, and repeat
Rotate the blank continuously while the cutter feeds
Index for all teeth first, then take one single cut
explanation: Feed the blank into the cutter to cut one tooth space, return the table, index, and repeat until all 22 spaces are cut.

question: What is the LAST step of the ME-106 milling procedure?
options: Polish (deburr) the gear with a file
explanation: The final step is to polish/finish the job using a file.

question: In the ME-106 milling job, how many times is the work indexed to cut all the teeth?
explanation: One tooth space is cut per indexing move, so a 22-tooth gear needs 22 divisions.

question: Why is the table brought back before indexing to the next tooth?
options: To reset the depth dial back to zero
So the blank is clear of the cutter while it is rotated
To let the coolant cool the blank down
To change the cutter for the next tooth
explanation: The blank must be clear of the rotating cutter before it is indexed, otherwise the cutter would damage the gear.

question: Which footwear precaution appears on the ME-106 milling log sheets?
explanation: Both milling log sheets and the TA slides say to wear proper/safety shoes.

question: While the milling machine is running, you should…
options: Touch the arbor to check speed
Keep a proper distance from the machine
Lean over the cutter to watch
explanation: Maintain a proper distance from the machine while it is on.

question: Which precaution about the workpiece appears on the 2025 milling log sheet?
options: Fix the workpiece in the machine properly
Rinse the workpiece in the plating bath
Coat the workpiece with pumice powder
explanation: Fix (clamp) the workpiece properly in the machine.

question: Which precaution is specific to indexing on the dividing head?
options: Do not lower the shaper head more than 2 mm
Check that the grinding wheel clears the work
Maintain a constant spark gap with the wire
Do not rotate the index-plate handle in the opposite direction
explanation: Turning the crank backwards introduces backlash errors in the division.

question: According to the ME-106 milling log sheets, you must stay alert during…
explanation: Stay alert during fixing and cutting.

question: Which electrical precaution appears on the ME-106 milling log sheet?
options: Switch on the machine only with wet hands
Do not touch any electrical connections
Open the control panel to check the wiring
Always touch the earth wire before starting
explanation: The 2022 milling log sheet says not to touch any electrical connections.

question: Which of these should be avoided while milling, according to the TA slides?
options: Safety shoes with steel toe caps
explanation: Loose items can be caught by the rotating cutter or arbor.

question: According to the milling TA slides, the machine should NOT be operated…
options: With the cutter guard in place
explanation: Do not operate the machine without supervision; clean the machine and workspace after use.

question: What should you do after finishing work on the milling machine?
options: Leave the chips on the table
explanation: The TA slides ask you to clean the machine and workspace after use.

question: Chips on the milling table should be removed…
options: By the coolant only, while running
With a brush, after the cutter has stopped
By hand, while the cutter runs
explanation: Never remove chips or measure the job while the cutter is rotating.

question: Which of these is NOT a milling-shop precaution?
options: Turn the index crank backwards to correct a mistake
Stay alert during fixing and cutting
Keep a proper distance from the running machine
explanation: Reversing the crank causes backlash errors. The other three are precautions on the milling log sheets.

question: Which is a typical application of milling?
explanation: Milling is used for gears, keyways, slots, flat surfaces of machine parts and dies.

question:
Assertion (A): Down milling gives a better surface finish than up milling.
Reason (R): In down milling the chip thickness is maximum at the start of the cut.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
explanation: Both are true. The better finish comes from cleaner shearing with no rubbing at the end of the cut. R states a correct fact but is not the explanation given for the finish.
ref: Milling lecture slide 7; Milling lecture slide 6

question:
Assertion (A): A 22-tooth gear cannot be indexed using only full turns of the crank.
Reason (R): In simple indexing the crank turns per division = 40/N.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
explanation: Both true, R explains A: 40/22 = 1.818 is not a whole number, so a fraction (27/33) must be taken on a hole circle.

question:
Assertion (A): In gang milling the cutting speed is based on the largest cutter.
Reason (R): All cutters on the arbor rotate at the same rpm.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
explanation: Both true and R explains A: same rpm means the largest diameter has the highest surface speed, so it limits the rpm.

question: Bevel gears connect parallel shafts.
explanation: False. Bevel gears connect intersecting shafts; spur and helical gears connect parallel shafts.

question: On a standard dividing head, 40 turns of the index crank turn the work once.
explanation: True. The worm wheel has 40 teeth and the worm is single-start (40 : 1).
ref: Manufacturing notes p.3; Milling lecture slide 22, s.25

question: The ME-106 spur gear is cut from a mild-steel blank.
explanation: False. The gear blank is an aluminium circular disc.

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled A?
explanation: A = Base. Heavy foundation casting supporting the whole machine.
label: A

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled B?
explanation: B = Column. Main vertical casting housing the spindle drive; carries the overarm.
label: B

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled C?
explanation: C = Knee. Slides up and down on the column (vertical feed) and carries the saddle and table.
label: C

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled D?
explanation: D = Saddle. Moves on the knee towards or away from the column (cross feed).
label: D

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled E?
explanation: E = Table. Carries the work and moves longitudinally on the saddle.
label: E

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled F?
explanation: F = Arbor. Horizontal shaft on which the milling cutters are mounted.
label: F

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled G?
explanation: G = Overarm (overhanging arm). Arm on top of the column that carries the arbor support.
label: G

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled H?
explanation: H = Arbor support. Supports the outer end of the arbor to keep it rigid.
label: H

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled I?
explanation: I = Spindle. Rotating spindle in the column that drives the arbor and cutter.
label: I

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled J?
explanation: J = Milling cutter. Rotating multi-point tool that removes metal.
label: J

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled K?
explanation: K = Elevating screw. Raises and lowers the knee.
label: K

question: In the figure, which label shows the knee?
explanation: C = Knee. Slides up and down on the column (vertical feed) and carries the saddle and table.
label: C

question: In the figure, which label shows the arbor?
explanation: F = Arbor. Horizontal shaft on which the milling cutters are mounted.
label: F

question: In the figure, which label shows the overarm (overhanging arm)?
explanation: G = Overarm (overhanging arm). Arm on top of the column that carries the arbor support.
label: G

question: In the figure, which label shows the arbor support?
explanation: H = Arbor support. Supports the outer end of the arbor to keep it rigid.
label: H

question: In the figure, which label shows the elevating screw?
explanation: K = Elevating screw. Raises and lowers the knee.
label: K

question: In the figure, what is the function of the part labelled D?
options: Moves on the knee towards or away from the column (cross feed)
Rotating spindle in the column that drives the arbor and cutter
Carries the work and moves longitudinally on the saddle
Arm on top of the column that carries the arbor support
explanation: D = Saddle. Moves on the knee towards or away from the column (cross feed).
label: D

question: In the figure, what is the function of the part labelled H?
options: Supports the outer end of the arbor to keep it rigid
Main vertical casting housing the spindle drive; carries the overarm
Carries the work and moves longitudinally on the saddle
Horizontal shaft on which the milling cutters are mounted
explanation: H = Arbor support. Supports the outer end of the arbor to keep it rigid.
label: H

question: In the figure, what is the function of the part labelled F?
options: Moves on the knee towards or away from the column (cross feed)
Horizontal shaft on which the milling cutters are mounted
Slides up and down on the column (vertical feed) and carries the saddle and table
explanation: F = Arbor. Horizontal shaft on which the milling cutters are mounted.
label: F

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled A?
explanation: A = Milling head. Carries the vertical spindle and its drive.
label: A

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled B?
explanation: B = Ram (overarm). Arm on the column that carries the head; can be moved in and out.
label: B

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled C?
explanation: C = Spindle (quill). Vertical spindle that holds and rotates the end mill.
label: C

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled I?
explanation: I = End mill. Cutter with teeth on its end and periphery, used for slots and faces.
label: I

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled F?
explanation: F = Knee. Moves vertically on the column to raise or lower the work.
label: F

question: Which milling method is shown in panel A?
explanation: A = Down (climb) milling. Cutter teeth move in the same direction as the feed at the cut; chip thickness is maximum at the start.
label: A

question: Which milling method is shown in panel B?
explanation: B = Up (conventional) milling. Cutter rotation opposes the feed; chip thickness starts at zero and is maximum at the end.
label: B

question: In panel A of the figure (cutter rotating clockwise), how does the chip thickness vary during each tooth's cut?
options: Maximum at entry, decreasing to minimum at exit
Zero at entry, increasing to maximum at exit
explanation: Panel A is down (climb) milling: the teeth move with the feed and enter the uncut stock at full chip thickness.

question: In panel B of the figure, the cutter rotates clockwise and the table moves to the right. Why is this up milling?
options: At the cut, the teeth move with the table feed
At the cut, the teeth move opposite to the table feed
explanation: With clockwise rotation, the bottom teeth move left while the work feeds right, so the cutter opposes the feed: up (conventional) milling.

question: Which milling cutter is shown in panel A?
explanation: A = Plain (slab) helical cutter. Machining wide flat surfaces with the periphery teeth (slab milling).
label: A

question: Which milling cutter is shown in panel B?
explanation: B = Side-and-face cutter. Cutting slots, steps and two parallel faces (straddle milling); cuts on periphery and both sides.
label: B

question: Which milling cutter is shown in panel C?
explanation: C = End mill. Cuts on its end and sides; used for slots, pockets and faces on a vertical mill.
label: C

question: Which milling cutter is shown in panel D?
explanation: D = Slitting saw. Very thin cutter for narrow slots and cutting off.
label: D

question: Which milling cutter is shown in panel E?
explanation: E = T-slot cutter. Cutting T-slots such as those in machine tables.
label: E

question: Which milling cutter is shown in panel F?
explanation: F = Involute gear cutter. Form cutter whose tooth profile matches the gear tooth space; used to cut spur gears.
label: F

question: Which cutter in the figure is used to cut the spur gear in the ME-106 lab?
explanation: F is the involute gear (form) cutter; its tooth profile matches the gear tooth space.

question: Which cutter in the figure is used on a vertical milling machine to cut slots and pockets with its end?
explanation: C is the end mill, which cuts on its end and sides. A (slab) and B (side-and-face) are arbor-mounted cutters for horizontal machines.
ref: Milling TA slides s.16; Milling lecture slide 19

question: Which cutter in the figure would be used for slab milling of a wide flat surface?
explanation: A is a helical plain (slab) cutter that cuts with its periphery.
ref: Milling lecture slide 9; Milling TA slides s.15

question: A pair of the cutters in panel B, mounted with spacers, would be used for which set-up?
explanation: Two side-and-face cutters separated by spacing collars machine two parallel faces at once: straddle milling.
ref: Milling lecture slide 12; Milling wall chart

question: Which milling set-up is shown in panel A?
explanation: A = Straddle milling. Two side cutters separated by spacer collars machine two parallel faces at once.
label: A

question: Which milling set-up is shown in panel B?
explanation: B = Gang milling. Several cutters of different sizes on one arbor machine several surfaces simultaneously.
label: B

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled A?
explanation: A = Index plate. Plate with circles of equally spaced holes used to count crank movement.
label: A

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled B?
explanation: B = Index crank. Handle turned to rotate the worm; 40 turns = one turn of the work.
label: B

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled C?
explanation: C = Index pin (plunger). Engages a hole of the selected circle to lock the crank.
label: C

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled D?
explanation: D = Sector arms. Set to span the required number of holes so they need not be counted each time.
label: D

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled E?
explanation: E = Worm (single start). Driven by the crank; turns the worm wheel one tooth per revolution.
label: E

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled F?
explanation: F = Worm wheel (40 teeth). Fixed to the work spindle; gives the 40 : 1 reduction.
label: F

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled G?
explanation: G = Work spindle / mandrel. Carries the gear blank and rotates it by the indexed amount.
label: G

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled H?
explanation: H = Tailstock. Supports the outer end of the mandrel.
label: H

question: In the figure, what is the function of the part labelled A?
options: Handle turned to rotate the worm; 40 turns = one turn of the work
Supports the outer end of the mandrel
Plate with circles of equally spaced holes used to count crank movement
Carries the gear blank and rotates it by the indexed amount
explanation: A = Index plate. Plate with circles of equally spaced holes used to count crank movement.
label: A

question: In the figure, what is the function of the part labelled B?
options: Carries the gear blank and rotates it by the indexed amount
Handle turned to rotate the worm; 40 turns = one turn of the work
Supports the outer end of the mandrel
Engages a hole of the selected circle to lock the crank
explanation: B = Index crank. Handle turned to rotate the worm; 40 turns = one turn of the work.
label: B

question: In the figure, what is the function of the part labelled D?
options: Set to span the required number of holes so they need not be counted each time
Engages a hole of the selected circle to lock the crank
Fixed to the work spindle; gives the 40 : 1 reduction
Handle turned to rotate the worm; 40 turns = one turn of the work
explanation: D = Sector arms. Set to span the required number of holes so they need not be counted each time.
label: D

question: In the figure, what is the function of the part labelled F?
options: Driven by the crank; turns the worm wheel one tooth per revolution
Set to span the required number of holes so they need not be counted each time
Fixed to the work spindle; gives the 40 : 1 reduction
Carries the gear blank and rotates it by the indexed amount
explanation: F = Worm wheel (40 teeth). Fixed to the work spindle; gives the 40 : 1 reduction.
label: F

question: The figure shows the 33-hole circle used for the ME-106 22-tooth gear. After the full turn, the sector arms span how many hole spaces?
explanation: 40/22 = 1 9/11 = 1 27/33, so the sector arms are set to 27 spaces on the 33-hole circle.

question: Using the 33-hole circle in the figure, how many full crank turns are made before the extra hole spaces for each tooth of the ME-106 gear?
explanation: 40/22 = 1.818…, i.e. 1 full turn plus 27/33 of a turn.

question: If the 33-hole circle in the figure were used for an 11-tooth gear, the move per division would be…
explanation: 40/11 = 3 7/11 = 3 21/33, so 3 turns + 21 holes on the 33-hole circle.
ref: Milling lecture slide 25; Manufacturing notes p.4

question: The figure shows a 21-hole circle used for a 14-tooth practice gear. How many extra holes beyond the full turns?
explanation: 40/14 = 2 6/7 = 2 18/21, so 2 full turns + 18 holes.

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled A?
explanation: A = Addendum. Radial height of the tooth above the pitch circle = 1/DP.
label: A

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled B?
explanation: B = Dedendum. Radial depth of the tooth below the pitch circle = 1.157/DP.
label: B

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled C?
explanation: C = Pitch circle. Imaginary circle on which mating gears roll; diameter = N/DP.
label: C

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled D?
explanation: D = Outside (addendum) circle. Circle through the tooth tips; diameter OD = (N + 2)/DP.
label: D

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled E?
explanation: E = Root (dedendum) circle. Circle through the bottoms of the tooth spaces.
label: E

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled F?
explanation: F = Circular pitch. Distance between corresponding points of adjacent teeth along the pitch circle = π/DP.
label: F

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled G?
explanation: G = Whole depth. Total depth of the tooth space = addendum + dedendum = 2.157/DP.
label: G

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled H?
explanation: H = Tooth thickness (on pitch circle). Width of a tooth measured along the pitch circle = π/(2·DP).
label: H

question: In the figure, what is the function of the part labelled A?
options: Width of a tooth measured along the pitch circle = π/(2·DP)
Radial height of the tooth above the pitch circle = 1/DP
Circle through the tooth tips; diameter OD = (N + 2)/DP
Imaginary circle on which mating gears roll; diameter = N/DP
explanation: A = Addendum. Radial height of the tooth above the pitch circle = 1/DP.
label: A

question: In the figure, what is the function of the part labelled B?
options: Radial depth of the tooth below the pitch circle = 1.157/DP
Circle through the tooth tips; diameter OD = (N + 2)/DP
Imaginary circle on which mating gears roll; diameter = N/DP
Circle through the bottoms of the tooth spaces
explanation: B = Dedendum. Radial depth of the tooth below the pitch circle = 1.157/DP.
label: B

question: In the figure, what is the function of the part labelled D?
options: Circle through the bottoms of the tooth spaces
Distance between corresponding points of adjacent teeth along the pitch circle = π/DP
Radial height of the tooth above the pitch circle = 1/DP
Circle through the tooth tips; diameter OD = (N + 2)/DP
explanation: D = Outside (addendum) circle. Circle through the tooth tips; diameter OD = (N + 2)/DP.
label: D

question: In the figure, what is the function of the part labelled G?
options: Imaginary circle on which mating gears roll; diameter = N/DP
Circle through the tooth tips; diameter OD = (N + 2)/DP
Total depth of the tooth space = addendum + dedendum = 2.157/DP
Width of a tooth measured along the pitch circle = π/(2·DP)
explanation: G = Whole depth. Total depth of the tooth space = addendum + dedendum = 2.157/DP.
label: G

question: In the figure, what is the function of the part labelled F?
options: Radial height of the tooth above the pitch circle = 1/DP
Distance between corresponding points of adjacent teeth along the pitch circle = π/DP
Radial depth of the tooth below the pitch circle = 1.157/DP
Width of a tooth measured along the pitch circle = π/(2·DP)
explanation: F = Circular pitch. Distance between corresponding points of adjacent teeth along the pitch circle = π/DP.
label: F

question: Which type of gear drive is shown in panel A?
explanation: A = Spur gears. Parallel shafts; straight teeth parallel to the axis.
label: A

question: Which type of gear drive is shown in panel B?
explanation: B = Helical gears. Parallel shafts; teeth inclined to the axis, smoother running with axial thrust.
label: B

question: Which type of gear drive is shown in panel C?
explanation: C = Double-helical (herringbone) gears. Parallel shafts; opposite helices cancel the axial thrust.
label: C

question: Which type of gear drive is shown in panel D?
explanation: D = Bevel gears. Intersecting shafts, usually at 90°.
label: D

question: Which type of gear drive is shown in panel E?
explanation: E = Worm and worm wheel. Non-intersecting shafts at 90°; large speed reduction.
label: E

question: Which type of gear drive is shown in panel F?
explanation: F = Rack and pinion. Converts rotary motion into straight-line motion.
label: F

question: Which type of gear drive is shown in panel G?
explanation: G = Internal gear. Teeth cut on the inside of a ring; meshes with a pinion on a parallel shaft.
label: G

question: In the figure, which panel shows gears on INTERSECTING shafts?
explanation: D is a pair of bevel gears, whose shafts intersect (usually at 90°).

question: In the figure, which panel shows gears on non-intersecting shafts at right angles with a large speed reduction?
explanation: E is a worm and worm wheel, the same type used inside the dividing head (40 : 1).

question: In the figure, which panel shows a drive that converts rotation into straight-line motion?
explanation: F is a rack and pinion.

question: In the figure, which panel shows parallel-shaft gears in which the axial thrust cancels out?
explanation: C is a double-helical (herringbone) gear pair: the opposite helices cancel each other's axial thrust. B (single helical) produces thrust.

question: Which panel in the figure shows the type of gear made in the ME-106 milling lab?
explanation: The ME-106 job is a spur gear (panel A): straight teeth parallel to the axis.
ref: Milling TA slides s.19; Log Sheets ME-106 p.9

question: Which Brown & Sharpe involute cutter number is used for the 22-tooth ME-106 gear?
explanation: Cutter No. 5 covers 21–25 teeth, so it suits the 22-tooth gear. No. 7 would be used for the 14-tooth practice gear.

question: For a 14-tooth gear, which Brown & Sharpe involute cutter number is used?
explanation: Cutter No. 7 covers 14–16 teeth.
ref: Theory: Machinery's Handbook; Manufacturing notes p.3

question: Before cutting the first tooth space, the involute cutter must be…
options: Offset to one side of the blank
Centred over the axis of the gear blank
explanation: Centring the cutter over the blank axis makes the tooth spaces symmetrical.

question: What is the correct way to set the depth of cut for the gear teeth?
options: Touch the blank with the rotating cutter → zero the knee dial → move the work clear → raise the knee by the depth
Zero the knee dial anywhere → raise the knee by the depth → move the work clear → touch the blank with the cutter
Move the work clear → raise the knee by the depth → touch the blank with the rotating cutter → zero the knee dial
Raise the knee by the depth → touch the blank with the rotating cutter → zero the knee dial → move the work clear
explanation: Touch off (e.g. with a paper strip), zero the knee dial, move clear, then raise by the calculated depth (≈0.1348 in for DP 16).

question: Which slide is used to put on the depth of cut for the gear teeth on a horizontal column-and-knee machine?
explanation: The knee is raised by the calculated depth using the elevating screw and its dial.
ref: Theory: Hajra Choudhury; Milling wall chart

question: Once the depth is set for gear cutting, which slides are locked?
options: Table only, leaving knee and saddle free
Knee and saddle, leaving only the table feed free
Index crank and sector arms only
Overarm and column, leaving all slides free
explanation: Locking the knee and saddle keeps depth and position constant; only the longitudinal table feed moves the blank under the cutter.

question: Before cutting the gear, the dividing head and tailstock centres must be…
options: Aligned with the table travel, with the blank tight on the mandrel
Removed from the table before the cut starts
Set at 45° to the table for a straight tooth
Loosely held so that the blank can slip if needed
explanation: Misalignment would make the tooth depth vary along the face; the blank must not slip on the mandrel.
ref: Theory: Hajra Choudhury; Log Sheets ME-106 p.9

question: If the gear blank slips on the mandrel during cutting, what happens to the gear?
options: Nothing, because the index plate corrects it
explanation: Indexing rotates the mandrel; if the blank slips, it does not rotate by the indexed amount, so the spacing is wrong.
ref: Theory: Hajra Choudhury; Milling Log Sheet #1

question: While the milling cutter is rotating, you should never…
options: Reach over or near the cutter
Watch the feed from the side
explanation: Keep hands away from the cutter path at all times.

question: When should the gear be measured or the chips removed on the milling machine?
options: While the cutter is turning slowly
explanation: Stop the machine before measuring, removing chips or adjusting the work.

question: On a horizontal milling machine, when should the arbor nut be finally tightened?
options: After the arbor support is in place
explanation: Tightening the nut without the outer support can bend the arbor. Also check the cutter rotation direction.

question: Which eye protection is recommended while milling?
explanation: Chips fly from the cutter, so wear safety goggles.

question: Which practice is correct on the milling machine?
options: Remove the guard so the cutter can be watched closely
Keep the cutter guard in place and use the correct speed and feed
Use the highest speed for every work material
Feed the work by hand into a stopped cutter
explanation: Guards protect against contact and chips; the speed and feed must suit the material and cutter.

question: Before starting the cut, you should check that the cutter…
options: Is touching the blank at the full depth
Is slightly loose on the arbor for safety
Is wet with dielectric fluid from the tank
Rotates in the correct direction for the set-up
explanation: Wrong rotation means the teeth rub instead of cut and can damage the cutter or work.
